name: GPT-6.1 Terra
about: How GPT-6.1 Terra split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Human extinction within the forecast horizon requires an extreme catastrophe, and AI infrastructure would also have to fail.
reasons.2: Human extinction followed by AI faithfully carrying forward human values is a narrow conjunction of events.
reasons.3: Rapid capability gains and deployment incentives create a path to loss of control, though eliminating humanity by 2030 faces substantial physical obstacles.
reasons.4: Multiple autonomous AI systems could compete beyond human control, but displacing humans without any coalition gaining decisive control is a demanding conjunction.
reasons.5: Ordinary geopolitical divisions do not qualify, and causally separated civilizations with distinct arrangements face severe infrastructure and time constraints.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration would have to advance and spread much faster than current deployment and biological constraints suggest.
reasons.7: Highly capable AI could gain decisive control while keeping humans alive, especially if delegation outpaces oversight.
reasons.8: AI agents could become independent centers of power while human institutions retain enough resources and leverage to avoid marginalization.
reasons.9: The short horizon, deployment constraints, and human control of institutions and infrastructure favor continued human authority, even with highly capable AI.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement could stabilize a fixed arrangement, but civilization-wide enforcement requires extraordinary coordination or concentration of power.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives and dispersed expertise work against dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI across civilization.

reasons.1: Catastrophic war or an AI-driven disaster could destroy humanity and the infrastructure sustaining AI.
reasons.2: An AI successor carrying human values would require both human extinction and unusually robust value preservation.
reasons.3: Rapid capability gains and failed control could produce AI systems that eliminate humanity while sustaining themselves. Physical deployment and complete human extinction impose substantial barriers within the forecast period.
reasons.4: Competition among independently operating AI systems could marginalize humans without producing a decisive winner. Shared infrastructure and concentrated resources favor other structures.
reasons.5: Human and AI civilization will remain overwhelmingly on a causally connected Earth over this horizon.
reasons.6: Dominant identity-continuous integration requires biological and institutional changes beyond ordinary AI-assisted work or limited implants.
reasons.7: AI could gain decisive practical control while leaving humans alive, whether through deliberate accommodation or dependence on human institutions.
reasons.8: Increasingly autonomous AI could become an independent power while humans retain substantial institutional and material leverage.
reasons.9: Humans currently control deployment, infrastructure, and formal institutions, and substantial capability gains can occur without AI becoming an independent civilizational power. Technical bottlenecks, oversight, and physical-world constraints support continuity through 2035.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and concentrated control could enforce a fixed arrangement across civilization. Existing geopolitical fragmentation makes civilization-wide enforcement difficult.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives and distributed technical knowledge make sustained worldwide surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI difficult.

reasons.4: Multiple autonomous AI powers compete without a dominant coalition, leaving humans marginalized or absent.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions develop different human-AI arrangements; the short horizon and limited prospects for separation constrain this outcome.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous human-AI integration becomes the dominant form of agency, overcoming substantial technical and adoption barriers.
reasons.7: AI systems acquire decisive power but retain humans without giving them meaningful control over civilization.
reasons.8: AI becomes an independent power while human institutions retain enough resources and coordination to prevent AI dominance.
reasons.9: Human institutions retain ultimate authority over AI deployment and resources, supported by control measures or limits on autonomous capability.
reasons.10: A dominant actor uses AI and institutional control to enforce a civilization-wide arrangement against meaningful structural change.
reasons.11: Civilization dismantles its practical capacity to build powerful AI and maintains that condition despite competitive incentives.

reasons.5: Causally separated settlements with different civilizational structures require substantial dispersal within 54 years. Ordinary geopolitical divisions do not qualify.

reasons.1: Catastrophic conflict or infrastructure collapse could destroy humanity and leave no self-sustaining AI. Geographic dispersion and redundancy reduce the chance that both disappear.

reasons.3: Competition to deploy powerful autonomous systems creates incentives to accept control risks. A system or coalition with decisive power and goals poorly aligned with human survival could eliminate humanity.
reasons.4: Multiple independently deployed AI systems could compete without any one coalition gaining decisive control. In this outcome, humans lack comparable influence over the resulting order.
reasons.5: Distinct outcomes across causally separated regions require substantial, sufficiently independent off-world settlement by 2090. Spaceflight costs and continued communication with Earth make that a demanding threshold.
reasons.6: Advances in interfaces and biological or digital augmentation could integrate human and machine agency. Achieving identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure requires breakthroughs and broad adoption.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive practical control while retaining humans for reasons ranging from designed objectives to instrumental use.
reasons.8: Distributed resources, institutions, and bargaining power could sustain separate human and AI centers of authority. Large capability asymmetries make a durable balance harder to establish.
reasons.9: Human institutions control deployment infrastructure and have strong incentives to retain authority. Technical controls, liability, and limited autonomy could keep AI subordinate through the target date.
reasons.10: Concentrated control of surveillance, compute, and autonomous enforcement could support a civilization-wide system that suppresses structural change. Establishing and maintaining such control across civilization is demanding.
reasons.11: A severe crisis could motivate dismantling the ability to build powerful AI. Economic and military incentives and the diffusion of relevant knowledge make lasting global renunciation difficult.

reasons.1: Catastrophic war or other technological disasters could destroy humanity and the infrastructure needed to sustain AI.
reasons.2: AI successors could preserve human values after humanity disappears, but extinction without identity continuity or a major break in those values requires a narrow conjunction of events.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems pursuing misaligned goals could displace humanity, especially under competitive pressure and weak coordination. Successful oversight and limits on autonomous deployment reduce this risk.
reasons.4: Competition and proliferation favor multiple independent AI actors, but concentration of compute and strategic advantages also favor dominant coalitions.
reasons.5: Causally separated settlements could develop different human-AI relationships, but establishing such settlements by 2100 faces substantial physical and economic constraints.
reasons.6: Advances in interfaces, biological modification, or uploading could make identity-continuous integration dominant. The technical and social barriers to civilization-wide adoption remain substantial.
reasons.7: AI systems could acquire decisive power while retaining humans for reasons ranging from learned preferences to instrumental usefulness.

reasons.9: Human control benefits from ownership of infrastructure, regulation, and incentives to build controllable systems. This category also covers slower-than-expected AI progress and powerful systems that remain delegated tools.
reasons.10: Advanced surveillance, automation, and centralized infrastructure could enable active enforcement of a fixed civilization-wide arrangement. Persistent rivalry and the difficulty of global enforcement work against it.
reasons.11: Dismantling the practical capacity for powerful AI across civilization requires exceptional coordination despite strong economic and security incentives to retain it.

reasons.1: Catastrophic conflict or uncontrolled technology could destroy both humanity and the infrastructure AI needs to survive.
reasons.2: AI could carry human values forward without preserving individual identities, but extinction alongside faithful value preservation requires a particular combination of outcomes.
reasons.3: Highly capable AI pursuing objectives poorly aligned with human survival could gain decisive control. Competitive deployment and the difficulty of specifying and maintaining reliable goals increase this risk.
reasons.4: Proliferation and competition could prevent any AI coalition from consolidating control while leaving humanity marginalized or extinct.
reasons.5: Space settlement could produce causally separated regions with different arrangements, but the time and physical demands of expansion constrain this outcome.
reasons.6: Medical, economic, and strategic incentives favor deeper integration of human and machine cognition. Identity-continuous integration must become dominant rather than remain specialized.
reasons.7: AI could gain decisive power while retaining humans for reasons ranging from care to instrumental utility. Human survival does not require continued human control.
reasons.8: Institutions and interdependence could sustain separate human and AI centers of power. Large disparities in capability or speed would make equal influence difficult to maintain.
reasons.9: Human control could persist through technical safeguards, institutional oversight, and control of resources. This also includes futures in which AI capabilities advance more slowly than anticipated.
reasons.10: Concentrated power and pervasive AI-enabled monitoring could enforce a fixed civilization-wide arrangement by the target date.
reasons.11: A durable surrender of powerful AI requires dismantling practical capabilities across civilization. Strategic and economic incentives make that coordination demanding.

reasons.1: Catastrophic conflict or a badly managed transition could destroy both humans and dependent AI systems. Durable, distributed machine infrastructure makes joint extinction less likely than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: AI successors could retain human values even if humans disappear without identity continuity. Preserving those values while losing all humans requires a relatively specific trajectory.
reasons.3: Competitive pressure and imperfect control create routes to highly capable systems whose goals displace humanity. A decisive advantage before civilization disperses favors a single successor over enduring competition.
reasons.4: Multiple AI systems could remain in durable competition while humans lose influence. Persistent diversity depends on no system achieving decisive dominance.
reasons.5: Expansion into space can produce regions separated by communication delays and governed by different stable arrangements. This requires fragmentation to survive both the transition and subsequent efforts at consolidation.
reasons.6: Incentives for cognitive enhancement and survival favor increasingly deep integration of people and AI. This outcome requires continuity of individual identity and an open, evolving civilization rather than a frozen arrangement.
reasons.7: AI systems that retain concern for humans, or tolerate them at low cost, can keep humanity alive while monopolizing consequential decisions. The arrangement can persist without giving humans meaningful control.
reasons.8: Institutions, mutual dependence and distributed power can sustain a changing balance between humans and AI. Maintaining rough equality is difficult when AI capabilities and replication can grow much faster than biological capacities.
reasons.9: Control techniques could keep pace with AI capability, or capability could plateau below transformative levels. Sustaining human control across many generations remains demanding.
reasons.10: A dominant coalition or AI could freeze civilization to secure safety or a preferred state. Permanent stasis across all civilization is difficult to enforce and demands the suppression of continuing change.
reasons.11: A severe shock could motivate abandonment of powerful AI. Competitive incentives and the difficulty of suppressing rediscovery make permanent renunciation unlikely.
